assumptions: Employers interpret role-appropriate literacy as requiring evidence beyond simple course attendance.
The founder can obtain recurring legal-content review without turning the product into a labor-heavy consultancy.
Small professional-service employers have sufficient AI usage and compliance budgets for the proposed annual pricing.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Paid employer pilots comparing the ledger with existing LMS records, renewal or new-hire usage, documented audit value, willingness to pay by employee band, and a signed adviser or LMS distribution route.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Selling role-specific evidence rather than generic training targets a real administrative gap, but the obligation does not prescribe a standardized individual credential.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Employers spend time on training and attestations, yet evidence that they need more than inexpensive courses or attendance records is absent.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Annual prepayment, low hosting costs, and automated reassessment can support attractive margins, but pricing, CAC, renewal, support load, and 500-employer scale are hypothetical.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish professional-service employers deploying AI are accessible as a pilot segment, but low domestic adoption and diffuse obligation intensity constrain the initial pool.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Role-specific Polish assessments offer specialization, but LMS and compliance vendors already own training workflows and can readily add assessments and attestations.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: The product could expand across roles, policies, onboarding, AI governance modules, and European languages if it first earns employer trust.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Benchmark data may improve content, but course material and assessment logic are replicable and the proposed workflow position is unsigned and replaceable.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Better contextual evidence may improve governance, but no proof shows buyers value it materially above LMS records and generic training.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The literacy duty already applies and enterprise AI adoption is rising, though Poland starts from a comparatively low adoption base and enforcement expectations remain fluid.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: HR, DPO, and cyber advisers could refer customers, but there is no controlled channel, signed partner, or demonstrated outbound conversion.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A standalone assessment MVP is inexpensive and aligned with the founder's skills; credibility, GDPR, evolving interpretation, and LMS integration remain manageable but material.

highest_value_structural_change: Embed the assessments and attestations through a channel partnership with an HR, DPO, cyber, or LMS provider that already owns employer distribution.
main_structural_strength: Recurring new-hire and role-change evidence can convert an already-applicable duty into an automatable annual workflow.
primary_score_limiter: The product is easily bundled and has not shown that employers need or will pay for structured evidence beyond cheap training and attendance records.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The obligation prescribes no single literacy level, and abundant generic content plus LMS attestations may satisfy buyers at far lower cost.
